subject: Physics
description: Conduction, convection, radiation — examples, laws, common applications

questions.stem: Heat transfer through SOLIDS (metal rods, building walls) without bulk movement of particles is called:

options.option_text: Conduction (energy passes via molecular vibration / electron flow)

questions.explanation: CONDUCTION — heat flows through stationary medium by molecular collisions + (in metals) free-electron transport. Best in metals (high free-electron density: Ag > Cu > Au > Al > Fe). Insulators conduct poorly — air, wood, plastic, ceramic. Fourier's law: Q/t = −kA(dT/dx) where k = thermal conductivity. Wood spoons in hot tea — handle stays cool because k_wood is low. Cooking utensils have wood/plastic handles for this reason.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: The boiling of water in a kettle, sea breezes, and atmospheric circulation are all examples of heat transfer by:

options.option_text: Convection (bulk movement of fluid carrying heat)

questions.explanation: CONVECTION — heat carried by bulk movement of fluid (gas or liquid). Two types: NATURAL — driven by buoyancy (warm fluid rises, cool fluid sinks) — boiling water, sea/land breezes, monsoon. FORCED — driven by external pump/fan — central heating, hair dryer, AC. Convection currents drive ocean circulation (thermohaline), Earth's mantle (plate tectonics), climate patterns. Doesn't work in solids (no fluid motion).

questions.stem: Heat transfer that does NOT require any medium and travels even through vacuum is:
questions.explanation: RADIATION — electromagnetic waves emitted by all bodies (visible light only at ~3,000 K+; below that, mostly infrared). Doesn't need a medium → that's how the Sun heats Earth across vacuum of space. Stefan-Boltzmann law: P = εσAT⁴ (T = absolute temperature). Black body — perfect emitter, ε = 1. White / shiny = poor emitter / absorber. That's why summer-cooling roof paint is white; winter clothes are dark. Wien's law: peak wavelength ∝ 1/T.

questions.stem: A vacuum flask (thermos) keeps drinks hot or cold by minimising:

options.option_text: All three modes (conduction, convection AND radiation)

questions.explanation: Thermos design: (1) Vacuum gap between inner-outer walls — eliminates conduction + convection (no medium). (2) Silvered surfaces — reflect radiation back (low emissivity). (3) Cork/plastic stopper — minimises top losses. Together — tea stays hot ~12 hours. Invented by Sir James Dewar (1892) for cryogenic experiments; commercialised by Reinhold Burger (Thermos GmbH, 1904).
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Newton's law of COOLING states that the rate of heat loss of a body is:

options.option_text: Proportional to the temperature DIFFERENCE between the body and its surroundings (for small differences)

questions.explanation: Newton's Law of Cooling: dT/dt = −k(T − T_surroundings). Holds approximately when T − T_s is small (and the body's emissivity is constant). For larger differences, Stefan-Boltzmann (T⁴) dominates. Solution: T(t) = T_s + (T₀ − T_s) e^(−kt). Applications: forensic time-of-death estimation, cooling rates in metallurgy, radiator design. Hot tea cools faster than warm tea because dT is bigger.
questions.subject: Physics

questions.stem: Why are houses in hot, sunny regions painted WHITE?

options.option_text: White surfaces reflect MOST of incident solar radiation; absorb less heat

questions.explanation: White / light colours — high albedo (reflectance) → reflect much of the visible + near-IR sunlight → less absorption → cooler interiors. Greek islands, Rajasthan rural homes use white extensively. Black / dark — high absorption → stays hotter (good for solar water heaters!). Modern 'cool-roof' paints with very high SRI (>90%) save significant AC load. Radiative cooling paints (e.g., Purdue's white paint, 2021) can passively cool below ambient.

questions.stem: Among Ag, Cu, Al, Fe — which is the BEST conductor of heat?
questions.explanation: Thermal conductivity (W/m·K, room temperature): silver ~430 (best); copper ~401; gold ~318; aluminium ~237; tungsten ~173; iron ~80; mercury ~8.3; water ~0.6; air ~0.025; vacuum 0. Despite Ag being the best, Cu is most used in cookware/wiring/heat-sinks because it costs ~70× less. CPUs use copper heat-spreaders + sometimes silver-loaded thermal paste. Brass + bronze + aluminium alloys for budget applications. Diamond is the BEST natural thermal conductor (~2,000 W/m·K).
